To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the use of a single antibody is not the best approach to cancer targeting.

(1) the use of a single antibody fragment (Fab) for targeting of a tumour antigen is not sufficient, because the antibody fragment is rapidly eliminated from the bloodstream and does not accumulate in the tumour, and (2) a single Fab fragment is not sufficient because it is rapidly eliminated from blood and does not accumulate within the tumour.

(1) the tumour-to-background ratio is improved by the administration of a second dose of the same MoAb, (2) the tumour is more effectively targeted when the first MoAb dose is administered after a delay of at least 2 days, and (3) the tumour can be more effectively visualized when the first MoAbs are administered after a delay.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the optimization of the targeting of antibodies by using different approaches.

the development of new MoAb fragments with high tumour specificity and high binding affinity, which can be radiolabelled with short-lived isotopes and which can be used for the early diagnosis of cancer and for radiotherapy.
the development of a new approach to the study of the effect of the antibody on the binding affinity.
